textContent.text: The phrase "first lady of aviation" might bring to mind Amelia Earhart, the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean. For many years, however, members of the press often reserved this title for another woman. While Earhart captured the world's imagination with her daring flights, many people believe that Olive Ann Beech had a much greater and longer-lasting impact on aviation—even though she wasn't a pilot. Over the course of her life, Beech blazed new trails for women in the aviation business, receiving more awards and recognition than any other female in aviation history.

Born in Waverly, Kansas, in 1903, Olive Ann was a precocious child. She opened her own bank account at seven years old, and by the age of eleven, she was handling all of her family's finances. She even built a number of hamburger stands with her father, which she managed on her own before selling them for a profit. After her family moved to Wichita in 1917, Olive Ann decided to skip high school and enroll in a secretarial and business college.

In 1925, she accepted a position at the newly formed Travel Air Manufacturing Company. Here, she met and married one of the founders, Walter Beech. Soon after, the couple left to start the Beech Aircraft Company, which would go on to make some of the most luxurious passenger airplanes in the world.

For a time, Olive Ann handled the company's finances as secretary-treasurer, while her husband ran the company's operations as the chairman and president. But in 1940, while she was in the hospital giving birth to their second child, Walter was hospitalized with a medical emergency, and Olive Ann heard news that a group of executives was trying to take over the company. She immediately converted her hospital room into an office, running the business from her bed. She even installed a phone line that ran directly from her room to the factory. As the interim leader during Walter's illness, Olive Ann guided Beech Aircraft through the years of World War II, securing lucrative government contracts to build military aircraft and fueling the company's growth. Throughout the 1940s, Beech Aircraft expanded its workforce by thousands and multiplied its annual revenue.

pieces.text: When Walter died in 1950, Olive Ann Beech officially became the president of Beech Aircraft. There were very few women in corporate executive positions in the 1940s and '50s, but Beech was undeterred. She brought on trusted advisors and was quickly recognized for her leadership skills within the aviation industry. During the 1960s, Beech oversaw the development of a new aircraft called the King Air, which became a sought-after executive plane purchased by notable customers like Walt Disney and President Lyndon B. Johnson. Johnson even selected the King Air for his presidential fleet, which he relied on when flying from the White House to his ranch in Texas. During this time, Beech helped negotiate a contract with NASA for the development of cooling systems for both the Apollo and Gemini space programs. In the 1970s,
magazine named her one of the ten highest-ranking female executives in the country.

textContent.text: Beech sold the company in 1980 and retired two years later, but not before receiving the prestigious Wright Brothers Memorial Trophy, awarded to significant contributors to the aviation industry. She is also enshrined in the National Aviation Hall of Fame in Dayton, Ohio. Beech died in 1993 at the age of 89, but she continues to be remembered as the "first lady of aviation."

textContent.text: Though she went on to become one of history's first female African American millionaires, Madam C. J. Walker came from humble origins. She was born Sarah Breedlove in 1867, to parents who were formerly enslaved. Tragically, Walker's parents died when she was just seven years old. Suddenly orphaned, she left her home in Louisiana and went to live with relatives in Mississippi. Walker eventually married and had a daughter—but in another devastating turn, her husband died under mysterious circumstances. At the age of twenty, Walker found herself widowed with a young child to raise on her own.

Walker then moved to St. Louis, Missouri, where her brothers were employed as barbers. She found work as a laundress and cook but struggled to get by. In addition to her financial woes, the stresses of physical labor and a second marriage that ended in divorce caused Walker's hair to thin and fall out. Little did she know that her scalp disorder would pave the way for her later success.

In the early 1900s, Walker discovered a hair growth product created by an African American chemist and businesswoman named Annie Turnbo. After using it for a year, Walker's hair improved so much that she asked Turnbo for a job as a local sales agent to help sell the product. Turnbo agreed and hired her.

As one of Turnbo's sales agents, Walker moved to Colorado and soon married her new husband, Charles "C. J." Walker, who also happened to be a clever salesman. Before long, she changed her name to "Madam C. J. Walker" and established herself as a businesswoman in her own right, developing a formula for a new hair care product for African American women. Though the recipe was likely inspired by one of Turnbo's products, Walker frequently told customers that the formula was given to her by a stranger in a dream.

Like her husband, Madam C. J. Walker was born for sales. She would sell her goods door-to-door, at church meetings, and eventually through a mail-order catalog. She also bought national advertising in newly popular African American newspapers. The result of her hard work was stunning. Customers flocked to buy Walker's products, which now included an end-to-end hair care system featuring scalp preparations, lotions, and special combs. At first, her husband helped Walker with marketing, but they divorced as the business grew. Madam C. J. took full control of her business, and her customers couldn't seem to get enough of the "Walker System."

By 1910, Walker was running her own manufacturing company, with state-of-the-art facilities in Indianapolis, Indiana. At its peak, Walker employed forty thousand agents throughout the United States, the Caribbean, and Central America. These salespeople were almost exclusively Black women—and devoted customers. At the time, the service industry was the only employment option for many African Americans. Walker believed that encouraging her employees to become successful salespeople would give them a new kind of confidence. Walker also promoted philanthropy and education among her workforce. In fact, she was known to award bonuses to women who gave back to their own communities.

Walker Manufacturing Company's employees didn't have to look far for inspiration. Their leader demonstrated her largesse by creating hair culture programs at Black colleges and universities, donating money to build an African American YMCA in Indianapolis, sponsoring free-tuition programs for college students, and supporting civil rights organizations such as the NAACP. Toward the end of her life, Walker even revised her will so that two-thirds of Walker Manufacturing Company's future profits would go to charity. And she specified in the company charter that only a woman could serve as president. Madam Walker died in 1919, but not before making an enormous impact on women—and especially Black businesswomen—everywhere.

textContent.text: What do phones, tablets, vehicles, and pay stations have in common? Modern versions of these devices all use touchscreens. Instead of manually typing or pressing physical buttons, consumers have grown accustomed to gently tapping or gliding their fingers across a flat surface. Today, touchscreens are used to call friends, make shopping choices, pay bills, and even draw pictures. It may seem as if these screens are a product of recent innovations. But in reality, touchscreen technology has been decades in the making.

An early version of touchscreen technology was invented in 1965 by British engineer Eric Arthur "E. A." Johnson. Johnson, who worked for the Royal Radar Establishment, was looking for a way to help air traffic controllers make rapid decisions that could be communicated efficiently to pilots. Johnson's solution to this challenge was a system of wires and sensors that used electricity to record the touch of a finger on the surface of a television-style screen. This communication technique would come to be known as capacitive touch (CT) technology.

CT is based on the idea that electricity can flow through a finger to communicate with other objects, such as a screen or monitor. In addition to the screen itself, CT requires three components, each with a specific role. First, a material like copper sends a small but steady flow of electricity across the surface of the screen. Next, a finger or special stylus presses down on the screen, altering the electrical flow. Third, sensors determine exactly where the flow was interrupted, mapping each "touch event" on the screen. Today, most cell phones and tablets use a sophisticated version of Johnson's basic CT technology.

A few years after Johnson proposed these ideas, scientist George Samuel Hurst developed another approach quite by accident. Hurst, an atomic physicist at the University of Kentucky, began experimenting with electrically conductive paper to automatically record coordinate points during his research. But he discovered that this paper could do much more than help with his data collection. After a bit of trial and error, Hurst and his partners developed the Elograph, the first device using what became known as resistive touch (RT) technology.

While both are considered tactile technologies, RT works differently than CT. Instead of recording touch events by conducting electricity through the finger, RT screens sense actual physical pressure. With this technology, two very thin materials are sandwiched together, separated only by a tiny air gap. When pressure is applied to one side of the material—for example, by a stylus or a finger—the two sides touch, and a sensor maps where the connection took place. RT technology is often used in businesses, such as grocery stores and doctors' offices, where digital signatures are required. You can often tell if a touchscreen uses RT technology because it is softer and more flexible to allow for gentle pressing.

A few important improvements have been made since the early days of touchscreens. Modern devices feature sensors that can detect multiple points of contact and complex actions such as drag-and-drop and pinch-to-zoom. But little has changed in terms of the basic technology. Thanks to the early pioneers of CT and RT touchscreens, the modern consumer can scroll through photos with a flick of a finger, play video games without external controllers and messy connectors, and answer the phone by tapping a tiny wristwatch.

textContent.text: The ability to privately listen to music almost anywhere—from a crowded subway car to a peaceful forest trail—is a luxury most people today take for granted. Music lovers simply press play on their device, and off they go with their favorite beats filling their ears via headphones or earbuds. But a portable, private listening experience wasn't always this easy. Not too long ago, music was heard through the speakers of record players, boom boxes, and cassette players, and everyone within earshot was forced to listen. A private, individual listening experience simply did not exist.

Then came a small, handheld device that revolutionized the way people listen to music: the Sony Walkman. The story of the Walkman can be traced back to the work of Japanese engineer Masaru Ibuka. After graduating from Waseda University's School of Science and Engineering in 1933, Ibuka began his career at a company that specialized in developing film used in movies. In 1946, he cofounded the Tokyo Telecommunications Engineering Corporation, which was eventually renamed Sony. Between 1950 and 1960, Sony introduced a number of important inventions, including Japan's first tape recorder. This product paved the way for later models, including the handheld Sony Pressman released in 1977.

During this time of rapid development, Ibuka gave his designers an intriguing challenge. Because he traveled frequently, Ibuka wanted a device that would allow him to listen to music privately on long flights. His team went right to work, building on the design of the recently released Pressman. The first Walkman model, the portable TPS-L2, was launched in 1979, just two years after the Pressman. It wasn't much bigger than a cassette tape, had chunky buttons, and came with a leather case and lightweight headphones. Plastic versions would be introduced later, but the original TPS-L2 was made mostly from blue and silver aluminum. Some of its features were eventually abandoned, including dual headphone jacks for two people to listen simultaneously. And while the Walkman was based on the design of the Pressman, one key difference between the two devices was that the Walkman did not have a "Record" button.

Sony expected that, without the ability to record, the Walkman wouldn't sell as well—but they were wildly mistaken. Within the first two months of its release, Sony sold an impressive fifty thousand portable cassette players. Then in 1980, Sony released the Walkman in the United States, elevating it to iconic status almost overnight. Interestingly, vinyl records had always outsold cassettes, but that changed in 1983, thanks to the Walkman. In fact, Sony's device was so popular that other companies introduced products based on its design, and the word "Walkman" came to mean any type of personal music player.

Maybe even more remarkably, Sony's humble little device drove a significant shift in culture and lifestyle. Before the Walkman, wearing headphones and tuning others out would have been considered vexing or even offensive. But by the 1980s, it became socially acceptable to enjoy music privately in public spaces, and this mindset for the most part continues to this day.

textContent.text: Picture a snarling lion sculpted from dark chocolate, crouched and ready to pounce, or a box of colorful, hand-decorated bonbons in flavors ranging from caramel pecan to raspberry cream to dulce de leche. Making edible works of art like these is part of the work of chocolatiers. These specialized pastry chefs combine artistic and culinary skill to make desserts that are valued for both their beauty and their taste.

Most chocolatiers learn their craft by attending culinary school or working alongside an experienced pastry chef. Their rigorous training includes learning how to identify and work with the various flavors of chocolate. While it is the separate job of a chocolate maker to transform cocoa beans into chocolate, chocolatiers study and learn how to evaluate the qualities of cocoa beans in their raw form. It can take years of practice to notice all the flavor notes in a particular bean. Some have a floral taste, while others tend toward the nutty, spicy, or even fruity ends of the flavor spectrum. The trick for the chocolatier is to find the right cocoa blend to suit the final product. Will the chocolate need to be bold enough to stand up to a smoky center of chipotle pepper cream? Or should it feature softer flavors that blend well with delicate herbs such as lavender or rosemary? The best chocolatiers will know the answer.

In addition to understanding flavor, chocolatiers must master techniques that give their sweet creations the perfect appearance and texture. One important skill to learn is tempering, a process in which the chocolate is heated and cooled repeatedly to prepare it for use in a dessert. Properly tempered chocolate is shiny, moldable, and free of lumps—making it ideal for shaping and decorating. Many chocolatiers also become proficient in panning, a method for coating items like raisins or cherries with a smooth layer of chocolate. Finally, chocolatiers learn glazing techniques to add a beautiful, glossy finish to fruits and pastries.

The types of companies chocolatiers can work for are as varied as the confections they make. Large chocolate companies like Hershey employ teams of chocolatiers who design confections for mass consumption. Smaller chocolate producers task chocolatiers with crafting more distinct (and usually more expensive) offerings. For example, the Connecticut-based House of Knipschildt sells one of the most expensive pieces of chocolate on the market. Called La Madeline au Truffe, this extravagant creation is made by encasing a famously rare French mushroom within a mixture of seventy percent gourmet dark chocolate, heavy cream, sugar, and truffle oil. The decadent dessert is then rolled in cocoa powder, placed on a bed of sugar pearls, and sold for hundreds of dollars.

Regardless of whether you're enjoying the ears of a carefully hand-sculpted chocolate bunny or a chocolate peanut cluster from a heart-shaped box purchased at a grocery store, you are probably eating a product designed with care by a chocolatier.

header.text: To form the plural of most nouns, add -s.
If a noun ends in -s, -ch, -sh, -x, or -z, then add -es to make it plural.
If a noun ends in consonant-y, then drop the y and add -ies to make it plural.
If a noun ends in -f or -fe and the /f/ sound changes to /v/ when it's plural, drop the -f or -fe and add -ves to make it plural.
If a noun ends in -f or -fe and the plural form keeps the /f/ sound, just add -s to make it plural.
If a noun ends in -o, usually add -s to make it plural. However, add -es for the following exceptions: tomato, potato, hero, echo, tornado, volcano, and mango.
To form the plural of a compound noun, like sister-in-law, only pluralize the base word of the noun. The base word in sister-in-law is sister, so the plural form is sisters-in-law.

header.text: To form the plural of most nouns, add -s.
If a noun ends in -s, -ch, -sh, -x, or -z, then add -es to make it plural.
If a noun ends in consonant-y, then drop the y and add -ies to make it plural.
If a noun ends in -f or -fe and the /f/ sound changes to /v/ when it's plural, drop the -f or -fe and add -ves to make it plural.
If a noun ends in -f or -fe and the plural form keeps the /f/ sound, just add -s to make it plural.
If a noun ends in -o, usually add -s to make it plural. However, add -es for the following exceptions: tomato, potato, hero, echo, tornado, volcano, and mango.
To form the plural of a compound noun, like sister-in-law, only pluralize the base word of the noun. The base word in sister-in-law is sister, so the plural form is sisters-in-law.
